authoring: Questions drafted with an AI assistant (Claude) from data/pages.jsonl, before any retrieval run; every evidence_quote is checked automatically against the normalized source unit by `python -m src.run` (results/benchmark_verification.json). The student must review them.
split_rule: Split by topic before any run: test topics (release date, tempfile.mkdtemp, free-threading, zero-cost exceptions, itertools.batched) do not appear in dev. Leakage risk: t01 and d15 both ask about page-1 front matter; t02/t05 have the same 'what changed in module X' shape as d16/d17.
filter_rule: filter is context given by the user before retrieval (e.g. 'I am reading the 3.12 notes'). It only uses the `version` metadata read from each page's og:title. Strategy C applies it; A and B ignore it. Questions with filter=null run unfiltered in C too.
selection_rule: Fixed before reading test results: pick the strategy with the highest dev Evidence Hit@3; ties -> higher dev Hit@1; then higher coherence mean; then fewer chunks / lower ingest time.
hit_rule: A retrieved chunk is a hit if its (document_id, page) matches a gold option and it contains that option's whole evidence_quote (case/whitespace-insensitive).

questions.question: How much faster is Python 3.11 than Python 3.10?
questions.expected_answer: Between 10-60% faster; about 1.25x on average on the standard benchmark suite.
questions.evidence_quote: Python 3.11 is between 10-60% faster than Python 3.10.

alternative_gold.evidence_quote: Depending on your workload, the overall speedup could be 10-60%.

questions.question: How can I attach extra context information to an exception object that was not available when it was raised?
questions.expected_answer: Call BaseException.add_note() (PEP 678); the notes appear in the default traceback.
questions.evidence_quote: The add_note() method is added to BaseException. It can be used to enrich exceptions with context information that is not available at the time when the exception is raised.

questions.question: Which new standard library module parses TOML files?
questions.expected_answer: tomllib (PEP 680), new in Python 3.11.
questions.evidence_quote: tomllib: For parsing TOML.

alternative_gold.evidence_quote: PEP 680: tomllib — Support for parsing TOML in the Standard Library

questions.question: What is the concise way to annotate a method that returns an instance of its own class?
questions.expected_answer: Use the Self annotation (typing.Self, PEP 673).
questions.evidence_quote: The new Self annotation provides a simple and intuitive way to annotate methods that return an instance of their class.

questions.question: How do you declare a type alias with the syntax introduced by PEP 695?
questions.expected_answer: With the type statement, e.g. `type Point = tuple[float, float]`; it creates a TypeAliasType instance.
questions.evidence_quote: the PEP introduces a new way to declare type aliases using the type statement, which creates an instance of TypeAliasType

questions.question: Can an expression inside an f-string now use the same quote character as the enclosing f-string?
questions.expected_answer: Yes, since Python 3.12 (PEP 701); in 3.11 it raised SyntaxError.
questions.evidence_quote: in Python 3.11, reusing the same quotes as the enclosing f-string raises a SyntaxError

alternative_gold.evidence_quote: Expression components inside f-strings can now be any valid Python expression, including strings reusing the same quote as the containing f-string

questions.question: Can pure Python code create sub-interpreters that each have their own GIL in Python 3.12?
questions.expected_answer: No. The per-interpreter GIL (PEP 684) is only available through the C-API in 3.12; a Python API is anticipated for 3.13.
questions.evidence_quote: This is currently only available through the C-API, though a Python API is anticipated for 3.13.

questions.question: My project still depends on distutils. What can I do on Python 3.12?
questions.expected_answer: distutils was removed in 3.12; install the setuptools project, which still provides distutils.
questions.evidence_quote: the setuptools project can be installed: it still provides distutils

alternative_gold.evidence_quote: The third-party Setuptools package continues to provide distutils, if you still require it in Python 3.12 and beyond.

questions.question: How much faster do comprehensions run after PEP 709 comprehension inlining?
questions.expected_answer: Up to two times faster.
questions.evidence_quote: This speeds up execution of a comprehension by up to two times.

questions.question: Which decorator tells static type checkers that a method is meant to replace a method of the base class?
questions.expected_answer: typing.override() (PEP 698).
questions.evidence_quote: A new decorator typing.override() has been added to the typing module. It indicates to type checkers that the method is intended to override a method in a superclass.

questions.question: How do I turn on the experimental JIT compiler in CPython 3.13?
questions.expected_answer: Build CPython with the --enable-experimental-jit configure option (PCbuild/build.bat --experimental-jit on Windows); it is not present otherwise.
questions.evidence_quote: When CPython is configured and built using the --enable-experimental-jit option, a just-in-time (JIT) compiler is added which may speed up some Python programs.

questions.question: How many legacy 'dead batteries' modules were removed from the standard library in Python 3.13?
questions.expected_answer: 19 modules (PEP 594), e.g. aifc, cgi, telnetlib.
questions.evidence_quote: The remaining 19 “dead batteries” (legacy stdlib modules) have been removed from the standard library

alternative_gold.evidence_quote: PEP 594 proposed removing 19 modules from the standard library, colloquially referred to as ‘dead batteries’

questions.question: How can I go back to the old basic interactive shell instead of the new REPL?
questions.expected_answer: Set the PYTHON_BASIC_REPL environment variable.
questions.evidence_quote: To disable the new interactive shell, set the PYTHON_BASIC_REPL environment variable.

questions.question: Which copy module function creates a modified copy of an object, and how does a user class support it?
questions.expected_answer: copy.replace(); a class supports it by defining __replace__().
questions.evidence_quote: The copy module now has a copy.replace() function, with support for many builtin types and any class defining the __replace__() method.

alternative_gold.evidence_quote: Any user-defined class can also support copy.replace() by defining the __replace__() method.

questions.question: Who is the editor of this What's New document?
questions.expected_answer: Pablo Galindo Salgado.
questions.evidence_quote: Editor: Pablo Galindo Salgado

questions.question: What can the interpreter now suggest when a NameError is raised to the top level?
questions.expected_answer: Modules from the standard library (e.g. "Did you forget to import 'sys'?").
questions.evidence_quote: Modules from the standard library are now potentially suggested as part of the error messages displayed by the interpreter when a NameError is raised to the top level.

questions.question: Which new functions were added to the math module?
questions.expected_answer: math.exp2() (2 to the power x) and math.cbrt() (cube root).
questions.evidence_quote: Add math.exp2(): return 2 raised to the power of x. (Contributed by Gideon Mitchell in bpo-45917.) Add math.cbrt(): return the cube root of x.

questions.question: Which mobile operating systems became officially supported CPython platforms, and at which support tier?
questions.expected_answer: iOS (PEP 730) and Android (PEP 738), both at tier 3, in Python 3.13.
questions.evidence_quote: PEP 730: Apple’s iOS is now an officially supported platform, at tier 3. PEP 738: Android is now an officially supported platform, at tier 3.

alternative_gold.evidence_quote: PEP 730: iOS is now a PEP 11 supported platform, with the arm64-apple-ios and arm64-apple-ios-simulator targets at tier 3 (iPhone and iPad devices released after 2013 and the Xcode iOS simulator running on Apple silicon hardware, respectively). x86_64-apple-ios-simulator (the Xcode iOS simulator running on older x86_64 hardware) is not a tier 3 supported platform, but will have best-effort support. (PEP written and implementation contributed by Russell Keith-Magee in gh-114099.) PEP 738: Android is now a PEP 11 supported platform, with the aarch64-linux-android and x86_64-linux-android targets at tier 3.

questions.question: When was this Python version released?
questions.expected_answer: October 7, 2024.
questions.evidence_quote: Python 3.13 was released on October 7, 2024.

questions.question: Does tempfile.mkdtemp() return an absolute path when the dir argument is a relative path?
questions.expected_answer: Yes. It now always returns an absolute path, even for a relative dir argument.
questions.evidence_quote: tempfile.mkdtemp() now always returns an absolute path, even if the argument provided to the dir parameter is a relative path.

questions.question: Is the free-threaded build without the GIL enabled by default, and which executable runs it?
questions.expected_answer: No. It is experimental and not enabled by default; it needs a separate executable, usually python3.13t (python3.13t.exe).
questions.evidence_quote: This is an experimental feature and therefore is not enabled by default. The free-threaded mode requires a different executable, usually called python3.13t or python3.13t.exe.

questions.question: Do try blocks still have a runtime cost when no exception is raised?
questions.expected_answer: No. Python 3.11 implements "zero-cost" exceptions, eliminating the cost of try statements when no exception is raised.
questions.evidence_quote: “Zero-cost” exceptions are implemented, eliminating the cost of try statements when no exception is raised.

questions.question: Which itertools function collects items into even-sized tuples?
questions.expected_answer: itertools.batched() (Python 3.12); the last batch may be shorter.
questions.evidence_quote: Add itertools.batched() for collecting into even-sized tuples where the last batch may be shorter than the rest.
